items.prompt: Authentication answers which question?
choices: Who are you?
What may you do?
Where are you from?
items.explanation: Authentication establishes identity.

items.prompt: Authorization answers which question?
choices: Who are you?
What may you do?
Which device?
items.explanation: Authorization decides what an identified actor is allowed to do.

items.prompt: A hotel card opens the wrong room. Which check was missing?
choices: Is this card a real one?
Is this card still new?
Is this card for this room?
items.explanation: The card was genuine; what was missing was the per-door permission check.

items.prompt: Which step is authentication?
choices: Entering a password to log in
Being denied a refund
Opening only your own invoice
items.explanation: Proving who you are is authentication.

items.prompt: Which step is authorization?
choices: Verifying a password at the front door
Checking a user may refund invoices
Scanning a fingerprint
items.explanation: Deciding what an identified user may do is authorization.

items.prompt: A logged-in user can read every other user's data. Which check failed?
choices: Authentication
Encryption
Authorization
items.explanation: The login worked; the permission check was missing.

items.prompt: Can a system get authentication right and authorization wrong?
choices: Yes, they are separate checks
No, one implies the other
Only on mobile apps
items.explanation: Passing the first says nothing about the second.

items.prompt: In a normal request, which check comes first?
choices: Authorization
Authentication
Neither has an order
items.explanation: You must know who is asking before deciding what they may do.

items.prompt: A gym member logs in with a valid password and opens a report page meant only for staff. What is true?
choices: Login failed, since staff pages must refuse members
Login worked; staff-only permission was never enforced
Both worked, since a valid password proves permission
Permission worked, since the page loaded for a member
items.explanation: The password proved identity. Nothing checked whether a member may see staff pages.
items.reference:
Two different questions
authentication: who are you? (login, password, card is real)
authorization: what may you do? (this room, this invoice)
a valid login answers only the first
hotel: real card is not the same as right door
Why: being logged in proves identity, not permission.
items.learnMore:
Authentication versus authorization

Authentication establishes who is asking. Authorization decides what that identity may do to a particular thing. A system can pass the first perfectly and still leak data when the second is missing, as a genuine key card that opens the wrong room shows.

Common mistake

Assuming that because a request required a login, it was also checked for permission.
items.reflection: Think of a place where showing a valid pass gets you in the building but not into every room. What is the second check there, and who performs it?

items.prompt: Which pair correctly matches a question to a concept?
choices: 'Who is asking?' is authorization; 'may they?' is authentication
Both questions are authentication, asked at different times
'Who is asking?' is authentication; 'may they?' is authorization
Both questions are authorization, asked about different users
items.explanation: Identity and permission are different questions with different names.

items.prompt: What does IDOR stand for?
choices: Insecure Direct Object Reference
Internal Data Object Routing
Incorrect Domain Origin Rule
items.explanation: It names an object referenced directly by an ID with no access check.

items.prompt: What is missing in an IDOR bug?
choices: A login requirement
An ownership check
A strong password
items.explanation: The login exists; the comparison with the resource's owner does not.

items.prompt: Which edit is the classic IDOR test?
choices: Changing http to https
Adding a trailing slash to the end of the web address
Changing /invoices/48213 to /invoices/48212
items.explanation: Swapping the ID for a neighbouring one probes the missing check.

items.prompt: Who controls an ID value in a request?
choices: The person sending it
Only the server
Only the database
items.explanation: Anything in a request can be edited by its sender.

items.prompt: Does requiring login prevent IDOR by itself?
choices: Yes
No
Only over HTTPS
items.explanation: A logged-in user can still ask for other users' IDs.

items.prompt: Where can an editable ID appear?
choices: Only in the URL path before the question mark
Only in cookies
URL path, query string or body
items.explanation: Every part of a request is under the sender's control.

items.prompt: An IDOR returned 200 OK for a stranger's invoice. Was it a login problem?
choices: No, the login worked fine
Yes, the login was missing
Yes, the password was weak
items.explanation: The user was genuinely logged in; the object check was absent.

items.prompt: Which one-line idea fixes the pattern?
choices: Hide the ID numbers
Compare resource owner to requester
Make the IDs longer
items.explanation: The fix is a comparison, not secrecy about the ID.

items.prompt: A team swaps sequential invoice IDs for long random ones and adds no ownership check. Is IDOR fixed?
choices: Yes; unguessable IDs make fetching others' invoices impossible
No; anyone who obtains an ID can still fetch it
Yes; random IDs count as an ownership check
No; but only because random IDs are slow to generate
items.explanation: Random IDs reduce guessing but IDs leak (links, logs, shares). Only the comparison enforces access.
items.reference:
The IDOR shape
GET /api/invoices/48213 -> your invoice
edit the id: GET /api/invoices/48212
200 OK with a stranger's data
missing line: invoice.ownerId == user.id
Why: an ID the sender controls must be checked against the requester every time.
items.learnMore:
Insecure Direct Object Reference

IDOR happens when an endpoint trusts an identifier supplied in the request without checking that the requester may access that object. The identifier can sit in the URL, a query string or a request body, and the sender can change any of them.

Common mistake

Fixing only the URL parameter and forgetting the same ID sent in a request body.
items.reflection: Where else, outside software, does handing someone a reference number let them ask for something that is not theirs? What stops that?

items.prompt: PUT /api/profile with body {userId: 7, bio: 'hi'} edits user 7's profile and requires login. Vulnerable?
choices: No; only URL parameters can be tampered with by senders
No; requiring a login ties the body ID to the sender
Yes; the body ID is editable and unchecked against the requester
Yes; but only when the bio field contains scripts
items.explanation: The sender controls the body just as much as the URL.

items.prompt: Which test reveals an IDOR flaw?
choices: Request a resource ID without logging in at all and watch the reply
Log in with a wrong password and read the error
Request a nonexistent ID and read the 404 text
Log in as user A, request user B's ID, see if data returns

choices: Login-gated endpoints look safe, so the gap goes unseen
Encryption libraries commonly leak object identifiers
Browsers often rewrite IDs while sending the request
Databases return rows without consulting the application
items.explanation: The endpoint feels protected because it requires login; the second check is easy to forget.

items.prompt: RBAC permissions are attached to what?
choices: A role
A single file
A network port
items.explanation: Users receive roles and roles carry permissions.

items.prompt: An ABAC rule is built from what?
choices: A list of role names and the permissions each one holds
Attributes of user, resource and context
A list of IP ports
items.explanation: ABAC evaluates facts about the actors and the situation.

items.prompt: 'billing-viewer can view invoices' is which style?
choices: ABAC
Neither
RBAC
items.explanation: It is a permission attached to a role.

items.prompt: 'user.id equals invoice.ownerId' is which style?
choices: ABAC
RBAC
Neither
items.explanation: It compares attributes of the user and the resource.

items.prompt: Which model can say 'this invoice, not that one'?
choices: RBAC
ABAC
Both equally
items.explanation: Roles do not carry per-resource identity.

items.prompt: What is a role?
choices: A kind of session cookie
A user's password hash
A named bucket of permissions
items.explanation: Roles group permissions under one name.

items.prompt: Is 'only from the office network' a context fact?
choices: Yes, it describes the situation
No, it describes the user
No, it describes the invoice being requested
items.explanation: Context is a fact about the situation of the request.

items.prompt: Which question does RBAC answer?
choices: Does this particular invoice belong to the requesting user?
Can this kind of user do this kind of thing?
Is this password correct?
items.explanation: RBAC works at the level of kinds, not individual resources.

items.prompt: Rule A: 'managers may approve expense reports.' Rule B: 'managers may approve reports from their own direct reports.' What is true?
choices: A needs an attribute comparison; B is a role rule
A is a role rule; B needs an attribute comparison
Both are role rules, since both mention managers
Both need attribute comparisons, since both mention reports
items.explanation: B compares who submitted the report with whom the manager manages.
items.reference:
Two ways to decide
RBAC: role -> permissions (billing-viewer can view invoices)
ABAC: rule over attributes (user.id == invoice.ownerId)
RBAC: this KIND of user, this KIND of action
ABAC: THIS user, THIS resource, maybe this context
Why: roles are the same for every resource; attributes can tell resources apart.
items.learnMore:
RBAC and ABAC

RBAC attaches permissions to named roles and users receive roles. ABAC computes a decision from attributes of the user, the resource and the context. Both are useful; they answer different questions.

Common mistake

Expecting a role to say anything about which individual resource is allowed.
items.reflection: Think of a rule where you decide by job title and another where you decide by comparing two facts. When would you switch from the first to the second?

items.prompt: Rule A: 'librarians may remove books.' Rule B: 'members may borrow only if they have no overdue books.' What is true?
choices: A depends on a member attribute; B is role-based
Both are role-based, since both involve a library
A is role-based; B depends on an attribute of the member
Neither is a rule, since neither names a resource ID
items.explanation: B reads a fact about the member (overdue count), not just a role.

Roles are checked after the response is already sent

choices: RBAC is easy to audit; ABAC expresses per-resource rules
ABAC is easy to audit; RBAC expresses per-resource rules
Both models express per-resource rules equally well, differing only in naming
Neither model can express rules about the requester

items.prompt: What does 401 mean?
choices: We do not know who you are
You may not do this
The resource is missing
items.explanation: 401 signals missing or invalid authentication.

items.prompt: What does 403 mean?
choices: You are not logged in to the site yet
You are known but not permitted
The server is down
items.explanation: 403 means identity is established and the action is refused.

items.prompt: What is the first check in the flow?
choices: Does the invoice belong to the user?
Is the role allowed this action?
Is there a valid session?
items.explanation: Every later check needs to know who is asking.

items.prompt: What is the second check?
choices: Is this role allowed this kind of action?
Is there a valid session?
Does the invoice belong to the user?
items.explanation: The role check follows identity.

items.prompt: What is the last check?
choices: Is there a valid session attached to the request?
Does this resource belong to this actor?
Is this role allowed this action?
items.explanation: The per-resource check comes after the cheaper ones.

items.prompt: A role lacks a permission. Which status results?
items.explanation: The caller is known; the action is refused.

items.prompt: Which check did the invoice endpoint skip?
choices: The resource ownership check
The session check
The role check
items.explanation: It never compared the invoice's owner with the requester.

items.prompt: No session is present. Which status results?
items.explanation: The server cannot identify the caller.

items.prompt: A previously working request now fails because the session expired. Which status fits?
choices: 403, since the role lost its permission
401, since identity can no longer be established
404, since the session record is gone
200, since the endpoint itself never changed
items.explanation: Expired session means the caller is unknown again.
items.reference:
Checks in order, and what each denial says
A: valid session? no -> 401 (who are you?)
B: role allows this kind of action? no -> 403
C: this resource belongs to this actor? no -> 403
all pass -> request succeeds
Why: 401 means identity is unknown; 403 means identity is known and the action is refused.
items.learnMore:
Order of checks and status codes

Identity comes first because every later check needs to know who is asking. The role check follows, because it is cheap and independent of the resource. The per-resource check runs last. Two denials share the status 403 but fail different checks.

Common mistake

Returning 401 for a permission failure, which tells the caller their login is the problem.
items.reflection: Think of a queue with several checkpoints. What would go wrong if the one that needs your name came after the ones that look you up?

items.prompt: A billing-viewer tries to refund an invoice and the role lacks that permission. What happens?
choices: A 401 from the session check
A 403 from the ownership check
A 403 from the role check
A 200 because the session is valid
items.explanation: The session passed; the role check refuses the kind of action.

items.prompt: Does a role table have a column for which invoice?
choices: No, only kinds of action
Yes, one per invoice
Yes, one per user
items.explanation: Roles are the same for every resource.

items.prompt: Does a billing-admin role alone show every invoice?
choices: Yes, always and automatically, on every endpoint
Only if a rule says admins bypass ownership
No, never under any rule
items.explanation: The bypass is a clause someone must write.

items.prompt: What does a combined endpoint run?
choices: Only a role check, then it returns the data
Only an ownership check
A role check, then an ownership check
items.explanation: They answer different questions.

items.prompt: RBAC alone reproduces which bug?
choices: The IDOR invoice bug
A password leak
A broken TLS handshake
items.explanation: Roles cannot tell invoices apart.

items.prompt: What does ABAC add to RBAC?
choices: Faster logins on every request
Per-resource comparisons
Stronger passwords
items.explanation: Attributes distinguish one resource from another.

items.prompt: Which is a context attribute?
choices: The invoice owner
The user's role
Time of day
items.explanation: Context describes the situation of the request.

items.prompt: If both checks are required, what follows?
choices: Removing either reopens a hole
Either one is enough
Neither is needed
items.explanation: Each guards a different question.

items.prompt: How does an admin bypass appear in the rule?
choices: As a hidden default the framework adds
As an explicit written clause
As a database index
items.explanation: It is visible logic someone chose to write.

items.prompt: User 5 has role billing-viewer and requests invoice 48213, owned by user 42. The rule allows owners or billing-admins. What happens?
choices: Allowed; the viewer role may view invoices
Denied; user 5 is neither owner nor admin
Allowed; the session is valid and the invoice exists
Denied; but only because the viewer role is too weak
items.explanation: The role check passes but the ownership rule fails for both clauses.
items.reference:
What each model covers
role table: kinds of action per role, no column for 'which invoice'
ownership rule: user.id == invoice.ownerId
admin bypass: an explicit OR clause, not automatic
real endpoint: role check AND ownership check
Why: remove either check and a hole reopens.
items.learnMore:
Combining RBAC and ABAC

A role table has the same row for every invoice, so it cannot separate yours from mine. An attribute rule can. Real endpoints use the role check to gate kinds of action and the attribute rule to gate individual resources, with any admin bypass written explicitly.

Common mistake

Believing an admin role automatically sees everything. It does only if a rule says so.
items.reflection: Where in your own work does a job title open some doors, but a second fact decides the rest? Which of the two is easier to forget to enforce?

They can view no invoices at all
They can view only invoices they own
They lose their session on each request
items.explanation: The admin bypass was the only reason the role mattered here.

Combining RBAC and ABAC

A role table has the same row for every invoice, so it cannot separate yours from mine. An attribute rule can. Real endpoints use the role check to gate kinds of action and the attribute rule to gate individual resources, with any admin bypass written explicitly.

Common mistake

Believing an admin role automatically sees everything. It does only if a rule says so.

Audit every ID-accepting endpoint

A fix on one endpoint leaves its siblings exposed: exports, edits, bulk lists and body fields can all name the same resource. The durable fix is the audit question, applied everywhere an identifier enters.

items.prompt: Implement `isOwner(user, invoice)`: true when the invoice's `ownerId` equals the user's `id`.
items.explanation: The ownership check is an equality between the invoice's owner and the requesting user.

items.prompt: Implement `isAdmin(user)`: true when `user.role` is `"billing-admin"`.
items.explanation: A role check compares the role name to the admin role.

items.prompt: Implement `hasPermission(rolePermissions, role, permission)`. `rolePermissions` maps a role to an array of permissions. An unknown role has none.
items.explanation: An unknown role falls back to an empty list so the answer is false rather than an error.

items.prompt: Implement `authStatus(user)`: return 401 when `user` is null or undefined, otherwise 200.
items.explanation: No identified user means the caller is unknown, which is a 401.

items.prompt: Implement `canView(user, invoice)`: true for the owner or a `billing-admin`.
items.explanation: Either ownership or the admin role is enough, so the two facts are joined with OR.

items.prompt: Implement `isTeamMember(user, invoice)`: true when `invoice.teamId` is in `user.teamIds`.
items.explanation: Team access is a membership test against the user's list.

items.prompt: Implement `isSharedWith(user, invoice)`: true when `user.id` is in `invoice.sharedWithUserIds`.
items.explanation: Sharing is a membership test against the resource's list.

items.prompt: Implement `guard(isOwner, isAdmin)`: return 403 when both are false, otherwise 200.
items.explanation: The guard refuses only when both facts are false, so either alone allows.

items.prompt: Implement `canViewInvoice(user, invoice)`. Allow the invoice's owner or any user whose role is `"billing-admin"`; deny everyone else. Return a boolean.
items.explanation: Ownership and admin are independent paths to allow, so the result is their OR. Using AND would deny nearly everyone.
items.reference:
The check in code
owner = invoice.ownerId === user.id
admin = user.role === 'billing-admin'
allow when owner OR admin
guard throws only when BOTH are false
Why: ownership and admin are independent paths to the same allow.
items.learnMore:
Writing the ownership check

Compute each fact as a boolean and combine them with OR. Handle missing fields so a missing list or user fails closed. Order any status-code checks as identity first, then existence, then permission.

Common mistake

Using NOT-owner OR NOT-admin, which denies owners who are not admins.
items.reflection: Think of a small yes/no rule you rely on. What happens at the edge where one of its inputs is missing?

items.prompt: Implement `invoiceStatus(user, invoice)`. Return 401 if `user` is falsy, else 404 if `invoice` is falsy, else 403 if the user neither owns it nor is a `"billing-admin"`, else 200. Check in that order.
items.explanation: Identity is checked first, existence second, permission last. Without the first check, an unknown caller could learn which invoices exist.
